Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

vignette:
James, a 25-year-old salesperson, had always dreamt of a life filled with excitement and adventure. He grew up in a small town, but his aspirations led him to a bustling city, where he thrived on the fast-paced environment and the thrill of closing deals. However, his life took an unexpected turn when he was sent to a war zone as part of a humanitarian mission. What was meant to be a noble cause quickly transformed into a nightmare. During a routine supply drop, a sudden explosion shattered the calm, leaving James trapped in a scene of chaos and destruction. In those harrowing moments, he witnessed the devastation of war firsthand—the screams, the smoke, and the realization that life could be extinguished in an instant. 

Since returning home, James had felt as if he were living in a different world. The vibrant city that had once excited him now felt threatening and foreign. Nighttime, in particular, became a source of dread. He found himself hyper-aware of every sound, the creaking of the building, the rustling of leaves outside his window, and the distant sirens that echoed through the streets. Each noise was a reminder of the dangers he had faced, and he could no longer relax or find solace in the darkness. James often lay awake, haunted by memories of that fateful day, battling a whirlwind of fear and horror that left him feeling exposed and vulnerable. Despite being in a loving relationship, he struggled to share these feelings with his partner, fearing they would not understand the depth of his pain and the guilt that weighed heavily on his shoulders.

During the day, James attempted to carry on with his normal routine, but concentrating on work became increasingly challenging. The once-simple tasks of engaging with customers and making sales pitches felt insurmountable. His mind would drift back to the war zone, replaying the traumatic events as if they were on a never-ending loop. He often caught himself staring blankly at his computer screen, frustration mounting as he tried to push through this mental fog. The pressure of performing well at work clashed violently with his inability to focus, creating a cycle that left him feeling ashamed and angry at himself. 

While his friends and colleagues continued to enjoy their lives, James felt isolated. He avoided social gatherings, fearing that laughter and light-hearted conversations would only serve as a stark reminder of his own turmoil. The guilt he carried for surviving when others had not made it nearly impossible for him to engage authentically with those around him. His relationship with his partner was strained, as he withdrew emotionally, unable to share the darkness that enveloped him. He had come to believe that his trauma was a burden he needed to carry alone, further deepening his sense of isolation.

As weeks turned into months, the constant threat of his memories loomed large, coloring every aspect of his life. James wanted desperately to feel safe and whole again, but the shadows of his experiences loomed too large. It was a stark realization that led him to finally seek help; he recognized that he could not navigate this journey alone. The idea of discussing his trauma terrified him, yet he also felt a flicker of hope that perhaps, through therapy, he could find a way to reclaim his life and learn to feel at peace once more. James hoped to explore the possibility of healing, fearing that without help, he would remain trapped in a cycle of pain and avoidance, forever haunted by the ghosts of his past.
